messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David Mercer, a 51-year-old school principal, traced the beginning of his difficulties to the months when a sudden life-threatening illness took over his life. He had been used to moving briskly through hallways, settling parent complaints, stepping into classrooms without hesitation. The illness interrupted that identity with a series of hospital admissions, repeated examinations, and the sharp, clean smell of antiseptic that seemed to cling to everything. He remembered lying rigid during procedures, his body fixed in a position he could not easily shift, waiting for staff to tell him what would happen next. What remained most vivid was not a clear, orderly narrative of the illness but a sensory imprint: antiseptic in the air, the medicinal scent of alcohol on skin and gloves, and the dread that accompanied being examined while wondering whether his body was failing him.

In the months after he recovered medically, those sensory cues began intruding into ordinary life. Passing a custodian using cleaning products in the school nurse’s office, catching the smell of alcohol-based sanitizer in the front office, or needing even a routine medical examination could abruptly pull him into the emotional force of the illness. Often there was no full picture in his mind, only a surge of fear and helplessness that seemed to arrive all at once. At other times, if he tried deliberately to recall what had happened in the hospital, he found the memory oddly inaccessible, as though the event would not come when summoned but only when triggered. In those moments his body would tense and settle into the same constrained posture he had held during procedures, as if he were back on the examination table.

These episodes shook David’s sense of who he was. Each time the smell of antiseptic or alcohol hit him and he felt himself freeze, he took it as proof that his body was still unreliable and that he could not count on himself to stay steady. He had come to believe that the person he had become was unrecognizable to him: not the calm administrator others saw, but someone internally braced for collapse. The fact that the memories came as bodily states and raw emotion rather than a coherent story only deepened that conclusion. If he could not even call up the experience deliberately, but was instead ambushed by it, that seemed to him further evidence that he was no longer in command of himself.

Because he no longer trusted his own reactions, David began trying to manage every interaction in advance. Before staff meetings, parent conferences, or even brief conversations with teachers, he silently rehearsed what he planned to say, as if careful scripting might prevent him from being caught off guard by a wavering voice or visible distress. He also started avoiding medical settings altogether, putting off examinations and taking long routes to avoid the hospital campus near the school district office. When possible, he delegated tasks that might bring him near the school nurse’s suite if the smell of sanitizer was strong. Outside of work, he withdrew almost completely, ignoring calls from friends and family and keeping his evenings empty. In his mind, this retreat made sense: if he kept life tightly controlled and stayed away from reminders, he might avoid the sickening bodily pull of the memories and the humiliation of feeling unlike himself.

Instead, the habits narrowed his world and seemed to confirm his worst beliefs. The more he avoided hospitals, ambulances, and examinations, the more charged medical cues became; even a routine checkup felt intolerable because he had had so little contact with anything that resembled care. The more he isolated, the less he had any experience of himself as capable or recognizable in relationship with other people. Rehearsing every conversation before speaking gave brief relief, but it also kept alive the idea that he could not rely on himself spontaneously. He noticed that on days when he had spent extra time mentally scripting staff interactions, he was even more alert to the smell of hand sanitizer in the office or disinfectant in the hall, as if constant preparation left him scanning for the next sign that something was wrong.

At work this became increasingly visible. David still arrived early and kept his tie straight, but he avoided impromptu visits to classrooms and asked his assistant principal to handle a student injury because the mention of an ambulance made his chest tighten. If he caught the smell of alcohol wipes outside the nurse’s office, he would feel a rush of dread before he could place why, then spend the rest of the day inwardly preoccupied, trying and failing to put the illness into words. Those moments left him certain that his body could betray him without warning. He found himself thinking that a man who needed to script every exchange and cut himself off from the people who knew him best was not the man he had been.

He finally sought help after canceling yet another medical appointment and realizing he was more frightened of a routine examination than he had ever been of difficult disciplinary hearings or public conflict at school. What alarmed him most was not only the fear itself but the sense that his life was being organized around escaping smells, procedures, and the internal jolts they set off. He said he wanted to know whether he could become someone recognizable to himself again, and whether it might be possible to face his own body without feeling that it was an enemy waiting to turn on him.
